newsitem.title: INDIA: India temple "purified" after fire tragedy.
newsitem.headline: India temple "purified" after fire tragedy.

text.p: Thousands of chanting Hindus consecrated a 1,000-year-old temple in southern India on Monday, two days after dozens of worshippers died in a fire and stampede that raised questions about safety rules.

Devotees beat drums and blew trumpets during the ritual to purify the Brihadeeswara -- or "Big Temple" -- in the southern town of Thanjavur, 320 km (200 miles) southwest of the capital of Tamil Nadu state, Madras.
At least 40 worshippers died on Saturday when a fire broke out in an outer portion of the famous temple complex, setting off a stampede among panic-stricken devotees.
Most of the victims were trampled as thousands rushed to escape the flames, which started from a firecracker and engulfed a temporary shelter of synthetic cloth and coconut leaves.

Some 20,000 worshippers attended Monday's Kumbhabhishekam rite, which had been postponed from Sunday. The crowd was far smaller than the more than 100,000 worshippers who had been expected before the tragedy.

Holy water was poured on the nine spires of the temple, which was built in the early 11th century by the Hindu king Rajaraja Chola and has been classified as a world architectural monument by the U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation.
Shimmering water pots and shining tents stood in contrast to the ashes, burnt poles and melted pots at the accident site.
Visitors discussed the apparent absence of precautions to prevent the fire and stampede.
"There was only one fire tender," said Rajaram (Eds: one name), who witnessed the fire. "Considering the scale of arrangements, I think that was simply not enough."
Witnesses said there was only one exit and many of the dead were women, children and elderly devotees trapped by barricades set up to control the crowd.
"How could they allow the firecrackers to be fired when they knew such huge tents could easily catch fire?" one visitor asked.

Experts in New Delhi said the absence or lax monitoring of safety standards often contributed to large-scale disasters in India. In February, 204 worshippers died in a fire at a Hindu gathering in eastern India.

"It is shocking but very little monitoring is done in our country. At times one gets the feeling that nobody is bothered," said R.K Srivastava, a social scientist at the Centre for Study of Developing Society (CSDS) in New Delhi.
India has no federal fire safety regulations. The Bureau of Indian Standards has recommended a set of rules, but the 26 states are free to adopt or reject them.
"We regularly send the guidelines to the various states but then the rest is up to them. We cannot force them," said Sanjiv Chaturvedi of the Bureau of Indian Standards.
